title: What chief sustainability officers are prioritizing now: Report
gist: A survey of 103 chief sustainability officers finds 63% expect global sustainability progress to hold steady or accelerate over the next year, with the business case (64%) and cheaper technology (56%) as top accelerators and policy uncertainty (68%) as the top constraint. The result is 'green divergence' across markets, an AI paradox where ~75% see AI helping but 77% flag its energy and resource intensity as its worst impact, and an adaptation-finance gap where 85% expect more focus but 62% cite uncertain cost-benefit math.

insights.claim: A survey of 103 chief sustainability officers found 63% expect global sustainability progress to hold steady or accelerate over the next year, meaning the majority view inside large corporates is continuity rather than retreat, even as implementation pathways diverge.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Corporate sustainability spend is unlikely to fall off a cliff near term; fade narratives of a wholesale ESG retreat and focus instead on which jurisdictions and sectors keep funding projects.
insights.quote: 63% of CSOs expect global progress on sustainability to hold steady or accelerate in the short-term, though pathways to implementation diverge.
insights.locator: 63% of CSOs expect global progress

insights.claim: The transition is fragmenting into 'green divergence' — sectors and markets moving at different speeds according to their own mix of competitiveness, resilience, energy security and industrial priorities — rather than converging on one global pathway.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Underwrite climate-linked exposure market by market and sector by sector; a single global decarbonization assumption will misprice both winners and laggards.
insights.quote: The result is “green divergence”: sectors and markets moving at different speeds, through different combinations of competitiveness, resilience, energy security and industrial priorities.
insights.locator: The result is “green divergence”

insights.claim: Emerging markets are expected to take a growing leadership role in the sustainability transition, shifting the geography of where projects get financed and built.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Look for transition capex and technology deployment growth outside the traditional OECD core, including EM industrial and energy names.
insights.locator: Emerging markets are expected to play a growing leadership role

insights.claim: Over the next three years CSOs name a stronger business case for sustainability measures (64%) and cheaper, more applicable technologies (56%) as the two leading accelerators — economics, not regulation, is now the primary driver.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Favour transition suppliers whose payback stands on unsubsidized unit economics; their demand is less exposed to policy reversal.
insights.locator: The changing forces driving global sustainability

insights.claim: Policy uncertainty is the single biggest expected constraint on sustainability progress, cited by 68% of CSOs, ahead of short-term business pressures (61%) and international tensions (54%).
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Regulatory volatility, not technology cost, is the main gating factor on project pipelines; track jurisdictional policy stability as a leading indicator of deployment.
insights.quote: Policy uncertainty is the leading expected constraint on progress, cited by 68% of respondents, followed by short-term business pressures (61%) and international tensions (54%).
insights.locator: Yet markets and technology do not operate in a vacuum

insights.claim: Policy is becoming less consistent across jurisdictions even though it remains essential to create the conditions for investment and deployment, so the same technology can be investable in one market and stranded in another.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Geographic policy arbitrage is now a real driver of project returns; diversify transition exposure across regulatory regimes.
insights.locator: Policy remains essential to create the conditions

insights.claim: Commercial and sustainability goals are explicitly described as not always aligning automatically, with durable value depending on a company's understanding of the resources, infrastructure and supply chains it relies on.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Screen for resource and supply-chain dependency as a hard financial risk, not a reporting line item.
insights.quote: Commercial and sustainability goals will not always align automatically.
insights.locator: Commercial and sustainability goals will not always align

themes.theme: Sustainability reframed from compliance to P&L

insights.claim: Inside companies, compliance remains the dominant lens on sustainability for 65% of respondents, while only 41% say it is already seen as a source of business growth or value — a roughly 24-point gap between cost-centre and value-centre framing.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Most corporate sustainability budgets are still defensive spend; vendors selling compliance and reporting tooling have a larger near-term addressable market than those selling growth narratives.
insights.quote: Compliance remains a prominent lens, identified by 65% of respondents, while 41% say it is already viewed as a source of business growth or value.
insights.locator: The CSO’s role is strategic integration

insights.claim: Two-thirds of CSOs expect corporate decision-making to shift further towards shorter-term performance priorities, putting pressure on projects whose payoff sits beyond the strategy cycle.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Expect long-dated decarbonization programmes to be deprioritized versus fast-payback efficiency projects; position with suppliers of the latter.
insights.locator: two-thirds expect corporate decision-making to shift

insights.claim: The CSO's real leverage comes from improving the quality of decisions made elsewhere in the enterprise rather than owning them, because CSOs do not control the choices that actually determine sustainability outcomes.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Vendors that embed environmental data into finance, procurement and risk workflows will outsell standalone sustainability platforms.
insights.quote: CSOs do not own every decision that shapes sustainability outcomes.
insights.locator: This is why the CSO’s role is linked to innovation

insights.claim: Sustainability integration looks completely different by sector: in a bank it shows up in lending decisions, sector strategies, client engagement and portfolio allocation, while in manufacturing it reshapes product design, materials, procurement and supplier relationships.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Sector-specific tooling and advisory beats horizontal ESG software; the buying centre differs by industry.
insights.locator: In a bank, that can mean better lending decisions

themes.theme: AI's dual role: efficiency lever and energy load

insights.claim: Nearly three-quarters of CSOs expect AI and other digital technologies to support sustainability progress via risk-modelling, process and resource efficiency, and measurement and reporting.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: AI-enabled industrial efficiency and ESG measurement software have a strong, budget-backed corporate pull from sustainability functions.
insights.locator: Technology and adaptation rise as key priorities

insights.claim: 77% of CSOs identify the energy and resource intensity of AI infrastructure as AI's most significant negative sustainability impact, meaning the same leaders buying AI tools view AI data centres as their biggest technology-driven environmental problem.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Corporate sustainability scrutiny of AI power and water draw is a coming procurement constraint for hyperscalers and a tailwind for low-carbon and efficient compute offerings.
insights.quote: Yet 77% identify the energy and resource intensity of AI infrastructure as its most significant negative sustainability impact.
insights.locator: Yet 77% identify the energy and resource intensity

insights.claim: Schneider Electric reports that its AI-enabled microgrid systems reduced energy consumption by 14% and CO2 emissions by 28% per site per year across 97 locations, a case surfaced through the World Economic Forum's MINDS programme.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified ROI benchmark for AI-plus-energy-management deployments; useful as a proof point for the industrial-software and microgrid names selling into this use case.
insights.quote: Schneider Electric reports that its AI-enabled microgrid systems reduced energy consumption by 14% and CO₂ emissions by 28% per site per year across 97 locations.
insights.locator: A case study from the World Economic Forum’s MINDS programme

insights.claim: In the Schneider Electric case, AI was applied to an operational challenge first, with sustainability gains emerging as a by-product of better energy and resource management rather than as the stated goal.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The adoption path that scales is operations-led, not sustainability-led; back products sold on cost savings that book emissions reductions as a bonus.
insights.quote: AI was applied to an operational challenge, with sustainability gains emerging through better management of energy and resources.
insights.locator: AI was applied to an operational challenge

insights.claim: Technology is framed as an amplifier of the strategies, capabilities and systems already around it, so AI's sustainability payoff depends on data quality, governance, infrastructure and measurable outcomes rather than on the model itself.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Value accrues to the data, governance and integration layer around AI deployments, not to raw model access.
insights.quote: Technology amplifies the strategies, capabilities and systems around it.
insights.locator: The survey insights do not resolve AI’s wider trade-offs

insights.claim: 85% of CSOs expect climate adaptation to become a greater global focus and 77% say private investment will be decisive in funding it, placing the burden of resilience spending on corporate balance sheets rather than public budgets.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Adaptation and resilience is the next growth category in climate capital allocation; watch for private capital vehicles targeting physical-risk mitigation.
insights.quote: Eighty-five per cent of CSOs expect adaptation to become a greater global focus, and 77% say private investment will be decisive.
insights.locator: Adaptation provides another

insights.claim: 62% of CSOs identify uncertain cost-benefit assessments as a major constraint on adaptation investment, because resilience creates value through losses that never materialize and therefore competes poorly for capital against projects with visible near-term revenues.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The bottleneck in adaptation is measurement and underwriting, not appetite; the first credible tools for quantifying avoided losses unlock the capital.
insights.quote: Resilience often creates value through losses that never materialize, making it harder to compete for capital against projects with visible near-term revenues.
insights.locator: Resilience often creates value through losses

insights.claim: Making resilience investable is said to require better risk modelling, credible business cases, clearer revenue or repayment models and risk-sharing mechanisms — a specific checklist of what is currently missing from the adaptation market.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Maps the product gap for insurers, catastrophe modellers and blended-finance structurers targeting adaptation.
insights.locator: Making resilience investable will require

insights.claim: The most consequential sustainability decisions are not labelled as sustainability decisions at all — they are choices about where to build, what to source, which technologies to deploy, how to design products and which risks to price.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Assess a company's climate exposure through its capex, siting and sourcing decisions rather than its sustainability disclosures.
insights.quote: The most consequential sustainability decisions are often not labelled as “sustainability decisions”.
insights.locator: The most consequential sustainability decisions

insights.claim: A factory, data centre, building, supply contract or product platform can outlast the strategy cycle that approved it, locking in costs, resource use, resilience and room to manoeuvre for years or decades.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Long-lived asset decisions made in a high-uncertainty policy environment are where stranding risk accumulates; scrutinize current capex cycles in heavy industry and data centres.
insights.quote: A factory, data centre, building, supply contract or product platform can outlast the strategy cycle that approved it.
insights.locator: A factory, data centre, building

insights.claim: Decisions that improve productivity or open markets while strengthening resilience are more likely to endure, while those that lock in resource exposure or physical risk narrow a company's future options.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Use optionality preserved versus foreclosed as a screening test on capital-intensive businesses.
insights.locator: Decisions that improve productivity or open markets
